children.text: The seat of the Archdiocese of Jaro and the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Candles, completed in

. A Marian image personally crowned by a pope stands on the balcony above the front stairs, and a bell tower rises on its own across the street, so in half a day you can also see the plaza and the old mansions.

The official name of Jaro Cathedral is the Metropolitan Cathedral of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, but it is more often called the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Candles. It faces Jaro Plaza in the Jaro district, about
4km
north of downtown Iloilo City. Jaro was an independent town until it was absorbed into Iloilo City in
, and because families who grew rich on the sugar trade settled here, many old mansions still stand around the plaza.
The faith community here began in the days of the Augustinian missions and became a parish in
. When the Diocese of Jaro was created in
, its first bishop, Mariano Cuartero, began building a new church in
and completed it in
. After the Lady Caycay earthquake of
January 1948
badly damaged it, the first archbishop, José María Cuenco, had it restored in
. A historical marker beside the façade notes that Graciano López Jaena, the orator of the Philippine reform movement, was baptized in this church in

The building is in the Romanesque Revival style with repeated round arches, and twin white towers rise above its gray stone façade. In the middle of the façade, stairs climb from both sides to a balcony, where the image of Our Lady of the Candles is enshrined in a glass niche. Pope John Paul II crowned it with his own hands during his visit to the Philippines in
February 1981
, and it is regarded as the only Marian image in the Philippines crowned by a pope in person rather than through a delegate. It was proclaimed patroness of the Western Visayas region in
and became a national shrine on
February 2, 2012
The church's other symbol is the bell tower standing on its own in the plaza across the street. First built in
, the tower is about
tall; the old church beside it was lost to an earthquake and only the tower survived, which is why a busy road now separates it from the cathedral. Its upper floors collapsed in the
earthquake, and after the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) completed its restoration in

, its bells ring again. The church, bell tower, plaza and old mansions are all within walking distance, making this a good fit for travelers who want to add half a day to an Iloilo City itinerary or who are interested in Filipino Catholic culture and Spanish-era architecture.

Climb the stairs on either side of the façade to see the image of Our Lady of the Candles up close in its glass niche. Carved from limestone, the Virgin holds a candle and carries the Child Jesus, and legend has it that the image kept growing until it no longer fit its original place. Many people come here to pray, so stay quiet.

This three-story tower is built of limestone blocks below and red brick above, with a clock on each of its four sides and statues symbolizing the virtues at the corners. It is said to have also served as a watchtower against pirates. The interior cannot be climbed without permission, so admire it from outside.

blocks.title: Central aisle lined with male saints

children.text: If Molo Church is famous for its female saints, Jaro Cathedral has a male saint on every pillar of the central aisle, with the Virgin Mary as the only exception. Visiting both churches on the same day and comparing them is one of the pleasures of a church tour in Iloilo.

See the high altar with the Virgin in a golden niche and the statues of Saint Peter and Saint Paul on the pillars to either side. The four corners beneath the crossing dome are painted with the Evangelists, worth taking your time to look up at.

The plaza has a white pavilion and fountain, a monument to Graciano López Jaena and a statue of Patrocinio Gamboa, a heroine of the revolution. The plaza was spruced up along with the restoration of the bell tower in
, making for a pleasant walk at dusk.
On E. Lopez Street, about
southeast of the plaza, Nelly's Garden, built by the Lopez family in
, can be seen beyond a wide lawn, and on Washington Street north of the plaza stands the Old Jaro Municipal Hall from
in Art Deco style. Most are private homes or government buildings, so you mainly see them from outside.

Jaro is known for biscocho, bread brushed with butter and sugar and baked until crisp. At the old bakeries on Lopez Jaena Street north of the plaza, pick up Ilonggo treats such as biscocho, barquillos and pinasugbo as souvenirs.
It begins with a novena on
January 24
, followed by the coronation rite on
February 1
, and on
February 2
a Mass with the blessing of candles and a procession led by the Jaro Fiesta Queen. In 2026, 15,000–18,000 people were expected to gather in the plaza on the day.

children.text: Leave downtown Iloilo City by Jaro-bound jeepney or Grab (about
15–30 minutes
From the roadside on the plaza side, frame the cathedral façade and the bell tower in one shot, then cross at the pedestrian crossing to the cathedral.
Climb the front stairs to pray or look around at the Marian balcony, then see the male saints, high altar and dome inside.
Cross over to the foot of the bell tower and take a close look at the clock, the statues and the wall of mixed brick and limestone.
Walk around the plaza's pavilion, fountain and López Jaena monument, and see the exterior of the Old Jaro Municipal Hall.
Walk to E. Lopez Street and view the Nelly's Garden mansion from outside the fence.
Buy biscocho at a bakery and take one more look at the cathedral and bell tower as the lights come on.
To avoid the midday heat of the dry season, it is easiest to look around early in the morning and move on to La Paz or downtown before lunch.
Arrive at the plaza and photograph the cathedral façade and bell tower in the morning light.
Look around inside when there is no Mass; if a Mass is on, sit quietly at the back and take in the atmosphere.
After a stroll in the plaza, walk along the street of old mansions and admire their exteriors.
Head to La Paz Market for a late breakfast of batchoy, or move on to Molo Church (about
15–20 minutes
by car).
Flights from Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO) take about
1 hour 10 minutes

, with several flights a day. There are also direct flights from Cebu. The airport is in Cabatuan, northwest of Iloilo, and Jaro lies on the way from the airport to downtown, so it is a little closer than the city center.
From the airport toward downtown, UV Express vans cost about
one way, and taxis or Grab about
(2025–2026 information). It takes about
30–45 minutes
to Jaro.
From downtown, take a jeepney with a "JARO" route sign and get off at Jaro Plaza. It takes about
15–30 minutes
, and since the fare adjustment at the end of September 2026, the base fare is about
for traditional jeepneys and about
for modern ones (for the first
4km
There are several Jaro routes, and some do not pass the plaza. When boarding, say "Jaro Plaza" or "Jaro Cathedral" and confirm with the driver.
A taxi or Grab from downtown costs around
. Enter "Jaro Metropolitan Cathedral" or "Jaro Plaza" as the destination. During rush hour and festivals, traffic makes the trip longer.
For short hops from the plaza to the street of old mansions or the bakeries, a tricycle is convenient. Agree on the fare before getting in.
Long-distance buses and vans from Kalibo, Caticlan (Boracay) and Roxas arrive at the Tagbak Terminal in the Jaro district. The trip takes about
3–3.5 hours
from Kalibo and about
2–3 hours
from Roxas.
From Tagbak Terminal to Jaro Plaza is about
10–20 minutes
by taxi or jeepney, so it is convenient to stop here first before heading downtown.
From Bacolod on Negros, fast craft reach Iloilo port in about
1 hour
, with fares of about
depending on the operator and seat class. Trips are canceled in bad weather, so check the latest schedule.
From the port to Jaro is about
20–30 minutes
by taxi or Grab.
The dry season from
December
to
May
is the best time to walk around the plaza and the street of old mansions.
December–February
brings relatively cool mornings and evenings, while in
March–May
daytime temperatures climb to around
, making midday walking hard. In this period, go outside before
or after
, and rest inside the church during the hottest hours.
From
June
to
November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, but the cathedral and bell tower can be seen in half a day, so you can easily visit between showers. Typhoons mostly affect the area in
August–November
, and when heavy rain coincides with high tide, roads in low-lying areas such as Jaro can flood.
The biggest event is the Candelaria Festival on
February 2

. It falls in the middle of the dry season, so the weather is good, but pilgrims, vendors and traffic controls make the area around the plaza very crowded. Dinagyang, Iloilo's biggest festival, is held around the fourth Sunday of
January
, so accommodation fills up early from
late January to early February
when the two festivals follow each other. During Holy Week in
March–April
, many special rites mean more hours when sightseeing inside is difficult.

There is accommodation in the Jaro district too, but most visitors stay downtown in Iloilo City (around Calle Real and the riverside Esplanade) or in the new Mandurriao district with its malls and restaurants, and visit from there. Both are
15–30 minutes
from Jaro by car. Mid-range hotels cost about
a night, and small guesthouses about
. During the Candelaria Festival and Dinagyang weeks, rates rise and rooms fill up early.

The thing to taste in Jaro is biscocho, bread brushed with butter and sugar and baked again until crisp; Jaro's old bakeries near the plaza have been baking it for generations. They also sell barquillos, thin rolled wafers, and pinasugbo, thin slices of fried banana coated in caramelized sugar. For a meal, it works well to eat La Paz batchoy, Iloilo's signature noodle soup, at the market in La Paz, the neighboring district to the southeast, or to head down to Molo for pancit molo, a dumpling soup. A bowl of batchoy costs about
Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees. If you are stopping by during a beach trip, keep a light layer or scarf in your bag.
Seeing just the cathedral, bell tower and plaza takes
45 minutes–1 hour 15 minutes
. Adding the street of old mansions and the bakeries makes it a half-day outing.

Mass schedules change often around feast days, Holy Week and Christmas, and an official schedule is hard to find. Check the cathedral's Facebook notices or ask the parish office in advance, and do your sightseeing between Masses.
To get the bell tower and cathedral in one shot, shoot from the roadside on the plaza side; the mood is best around
when the lights come on.
The female saints of Molo Church and the male saints of Jaro Cathedral are a matching pair of sights. The two are
15–20 minutes
apart by car, so they combine well on the same day.
The Marian balcony can only be reached by stairs, and there is no wheelchair access. If you have limited mobility, the image can be seen well from the foot of the stairs.
If you are going for the festival on
February 2
, arrive in time for the coronation rite the evening before or an early-morning Mass on the day, and leave your car far away and walk in.
Bring plenty of small bills (₱20, ₱50) for jeepney and tricycle fares. Offerings in the donation box and candle offerings are optional.

Before it is a tourist sight, Jaro Cathedral is a metropolitan cathedral and a national shrine. Visits inside may be restricted without notice during Masses, weddings, funerals or diocesan events, so on such days focus on the exterior and the plaza and come back another time for the interior.
The busy road between the cathedral and the bell tower carries heavy jeepney and car traffic. Do not step into the road while taking photos; cross at the pedestrian crossing.
The bell tower is a heritage structure, so do not enter or climb it without permission. Do not touch the Marian image, the statues of saints or the altar decorations.
During Mass, do not walk along the central aisle or photograph people receiving communion. Do not use flash, tripods or drones without the parish's permission.
During the festival on
February 1–2
, roads are closed and it gets so crowded that schools in the Jaro district suspend classes. Watch out for pickpockets and leave slack in your schedule.
The plaza has little shade at midday and there is a risk of heatstroke, so bring water and a hat; in the rainy season, carry an umbrella and check for flood news.
